body.text: Statutory Construction, Site-Specific Experimentation, and Evidentiary Governance Under the Australian R&D Tax Incentive: A Legal and Technical Analysis of Moreton Resources Ltd v Innovation and Science Australia [2019] FCAFC 120

1. Executive Summary & Case Background
1.1 Overview of the Proceeding and Jurisprudential Significance
The judgment of the Full Court of the Federal Court of Australia in Moreton Resources Limited v Innovation and Science Australia [2019] FCAFC 120 (reported at (2019) 271 FCR 211; 165 ALD 420; 110 ATR 248; 2019 ATC 20-700) stands as the foundational appellate authority governing the statutory construction of "core R&D activities" and "supporting R&D activities" under Division 355 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth) (ITAA 1997)1. Handed down on 25 July 2019 in Melbourne by a unanimous bench comprising Davies, Moshinsky, and Steward JJ, the decision dismantled a restrictive interpretive orthodoxy previously enforced by the programme regulator, Innovation and Science Australia (ISA, now styled Industry Innovation and Science Australia or IISA, assisted by AusIndustry), and endorsed at first instance by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT, now the Administrative Review Tribunal or ART)2.
Specifically, the Full Court rejected the regulator's contention that experimental activities undertaken to generate new knowledge regarding the application of an existing, proven technology at a new geographical or geological site are inherently incapable of satisfying the statutory definition of "core R&D activities" in section 355-25(1) of the ITAA 19973. Furthermore, while the Full Court noted that section 27J(1)(c)(ii) of the IR&D Act permits the Board to find that an activity registered in one income year was a "supporting R&D activity" in relation to core R&D activities registered in an earlier income year (and that the parties did not dispute that activities registered as core R&D activities could be found to be supporting R&D activities), it expressly declined to decide whether Moreton's post-failure remediation, monitoring, and decommissioning activities were "directly related" to, and undertaken for the "dominant purpose" of supporting, the 2010 core R&D activities under section 355-30, holding that this factually intensive question should be remitted to the Tribunal3.
1.2 Corporate Evolution, Technological Licensing, and the Kingaroy Pilot Project
To evaluate the technical and legal posture of the dispute, it is necessary to trace the operational history of the taxpayer and its Underground Coal Gasification (UCG) project3. Originally incorporated in 1994 as Pinnacle Mining NL and renamed Pinnacle VRB Limited in June 1998, the corporate entity acquired Cougar Energy Pty Ltd in 2006 and changed its name to Cougar Energy Limited on 16 February 2007, before rebranding as Moreton Resources Limited on 11 October 20133. Beginning around 2006 and 2007, the taxpayer initiated a major industrial project to design, construct, ignite, and operate a UCG pilot facility near Kingaroy in Queensland, alongside secondary geological evaluations at Wandoan in the Surat Basin3.
To execute the project, on 3 November 2008 the taxpayer obtained from the Canadian engineering firm Ergo Exergy Technologies Inc. a general licence to certain of Ergo Exergy's intellectual knowledge, together with an offer of services to assist the taxpayer to undertake the research and development required to develop the technical viability of its UCG plant at Kingaroy; Ergo Exergy had some expertise in the burn process but held no intellectual property in the design, development, and operation of an integrated UCG power generation facility incorporating a gas processing plant and gas turbines3. The overarching technical and commercial objective of the Kingaroy pilot project was to test the viability of applying UCG technology to the specific coal seams at the Kingaroy site to produce synthesis gas (syngas) in situ, which would then be extracted, cleaned, and stabilised at the surface to fuel gas turbines for a proposed 400 MW electricity generation plant3.
Following preliminary geological characterisation, borehole drilling, and surface and subsurface plant construction, the UCG burn process at the Kingaroy pilot plant was ignited in well P1 at about 3.30 pm on 15 March 2010, with the first syngas detected within 30 minutes of ignition, during the 2010 income year (FY10)3. However, within days of ignition, the operational phase of the pilot facility suffered an unexpected technical failure: steam was observed at the base of the casing strings of production well P4 on 18 March 2010, the casing of P4 moved on 20 March 2010, and subsequent investigations revealed a solid blockage in well P1 at a depth of approximately 132 metres and a casing break in well P4 at approximately 62 metres, both believed to have been caused by thermal expansion and poor cementing between the inner and outer casings, whereupon the taxpayer shut down the plant3. After the taxpayer reported that water quality tests conducted on 29 June 2010 had detected benzene and toluene in groundwater monitoring bores close to the plant, the Queensland Department of Environment and Resource Management (DERM) stated on 15 July 2010 that it would order the taxpayer to keep the pilot project closed, and on 17 July 2010 it issued an Environmental Protection Order (EPO) to the taxpayer3. Although DERM's own testing of five of the eight bores concluded that the levels were below the Australian Drinking Water Guideline standards, the EPO required the taxpayer not to commence or recommence any burning of underground coal until further notice, to repair and seal the damaged well P4, and to sample groundwater from all known bores in the potentially affected area twice per week; DERM subsequently issued Environmental Evaluation Notices, on 7 July 2011 amended the taxpayer's environmental authority so that the approved activities were limited solely to decommissioning, rehabilitation, care, and maintenance of the site, and on 18 April 2016 the Queensland Government announced a ban on UCG because of its environmental impact3. After unsuccessfully seeking a stay of the 2011 amendment to its environmental authority (refused by the Queensland Planning and Environment Court on 21 December 2011) and, following the replacement of its board in 2013, discontinuing its proceedings relating to the Kingaroy project, the taxpayer, in September 2013, pleaded guilty to three counts of contravening the conditions of an environmental authority, incurring a fine of A40,000 in court costs3.
Consequently, across the 2012, 2013, and 2014 income years (FY12, FY13, and FY14), the taxpayer could not conduct active coal gasification, although it continued to plan for re-ignition (including a December 2011 restart plan) until its new board decided in June 2013 to cease efforts to reignite the project and abandon the pilot project3. Instead, its physical and engineering activities at the Kingaroy site consisted of investigating the root cause and mechanics of the underground cavity failure, modelling groundwater movement, conducting ongoing water quality monitoring, designing and verifying procedures for the rehabilitation of the underground cavity, environmental monitoring and rehabilitation, and investigating and developing engineering processes to decommission the pilot plant3.
1.3 The Taxpayer's R&D Claim and the Regulator's Challenge
Moreton Resources registered its FY12, FY13, and FY14 post-incident activities under section 27A of the Industry Research and Development Act 1986 (Cth) (IR&D Act) in order to claim the R&D tax offset under Division 355 of the ITAA 19973. In its registrations, the taxpayer classified the technical investigations, environmental monitoring, groundwater modelling, cavity rehabilitation design, and decommissioning process development primarily as "core R&D activities" under section 355-25(1), while classifying as "supporting R&D activities" under section 355-30 ongoing water monitoring, an environmental impact assessment for DERM, preliminary economic analysis, and pre-feasibility study work (FY12), project management and administration (FY13 and FY14), and environmental rehabilitation and planning (FY14)3. In the alternative, the taxpayer contended that if the FY12–FY14 activities did not independently satisfy the threshold for core R&D activities, they nonetheless qualified as "supporting R&D activities" under section 355-30 because they were directly related to the core R&D activities conducted in FY10—namely, the design, ignition, and experimental testing of the Kingaroy UCG pilot plant3.
Following a statutory examination under section 27F of the IR&D Act, ISA issued negative findings under section 27J (subsequently confirmed upon internal review under section 30D), determining that none of the registered activities in FY12, FY13, or FY14 constituted either core R&D activities or supporting R&D activities3. Because a finding under section 27J of the IR&D Act binds the Commissioner of Taxation pursuant to section 355-705 of the ITAA 1997, the negative findings extinguished the taxpayer's entitlement to the R&D tax offset for all three income years3.
In Re Moreton Resources Ltd and Innovation and Science Australia [2018] AATA 3378, the AAT (constituted by Deputy President Forgie) affirmed ISA's negative reviewable decisions in their entirety3. The Tribunal's disallowance rested on three interconnected legal conclusions. First, although the Tribunal accepted that, in the ordinary meaning of an "experimental activity", the pilot project could be regarded as such an activity (Reasons, [258]), it held that the pilot project as a whole was not an "experimental activity" within section 355-25(1) because, beyond the site-specific knowledge it would generate, it was not undertaken to develop UCG technology itself or any new form of pilot plant, devices, or processes, and was "testing the application of existing technology at a particular site and nothing more" (Reasons, [259], [262]); the Tribunal did not directly consider the registered FY10 activities, but its reasoning applied equally to them3. Second, the Tribunal determined that many of the FY12–FY14 post-incident monitoring, rehabilitation, and decommissioning activities were excluded from being core R&D activities under section 355-25(2)(f) of the ITAA 1997 because they were "activities associated with complying with statutory requirements or standards" imposed under the Queensland environmental regulatory regime (a conclusion Moreton did not challenge on appeal)3. Third, because the Tribunal concluded that there were no core R&D activities, it held that there could be no supporting R&D activities (Reasons, [328]), thereby implicitly rejecting the taxpayer's alternative argument under section 355-30 without determining whether the FY10 activities were conducted, whether the FY12–FY14 activities were "directly related" to them, or whether they were undertaken for the "dominant purpose" of supporting them3.
1.4 Governing Statutory Architecture in Australia
The dispute in Moreton Resources is governed by the dual-agency legislative regime introduced by the Tax Laws Amendment (Research and Development) Act 2011 (Cth), which replaced the former section 73B concession in the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth) with the R&D Tax Incentive codified in Division 355 of the ITAA 1997 and Part III of the IR&D Act3.

Statutory Provision
Legislation
Core Legal Function in the R&D Tax Incentive Regime
Section 355-5
Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth)
Establishes the statutory object of encouraging industry to conduct, in a scientific way, experimental activities for the purpose of generating new knowledge or information in either a general or applied form (including new or improved materials, products, devices, processes, or services) where returns are uncertain3.
Section 355-20
Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth)
Defines "R&D activities" exhaustively as comprising either "core R&D activities" or "supporting R&D activities"7.
Section 355-25(1)(a)
Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth)
Enacts the epistemological and methodological limb for core R&D activities: must be experimental activities whose outcome cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information, or experience, but can only be determined by applying a systematic progression of work based on principles of established science that proceeds from hypothesis to experiment, observation, and evaluation, and leads to logical conclusions3.
Section 355-25(1)(b)
Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth)
Enacts the purposive limb for core R&D activities: must be conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge (including new knowledge in the form of new or improved materials, products, devices, processes, or services)3.
Section 355-25(2)(b) & (f)
Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth)
Excludes specified activities from qualifying as core R&D activities, notably prospecting, exploring, or drilling for minerals or petroleum (para (b)), and activities associated with complying with statutory requirements or standards, including routine testing and analysis of materials, components, products, processes, soils, atmospheres, and other things (para (f))3.
Section 355-30(1)–(2)
Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth)
Defines "supporting R&D activities" as activities directly related to core R&D activities (sub-s (1)), subject to a strict "dominant purpose" test (sub-s (2)) if the supporting activity falls within an exclusion in section 355-25(2) or produces, or is directly related to producing, goods or services3.
Sections 27A, 27F, 27J & 30D
Industry Research and Development Act 1986 (Cth)
Governs the annual registration of R&D activities by R&D entities (s 27A), regulatory compliance examinations by the Board/IISA (s 27F), the issuance of positive or negative activity findings (s 27J)—including findings relating to core activities conducted in earlier or future income years under s 27J(1)(c)—and internal review of reviewable decisions (s 30D)3.
Section 355-705
Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth)
Renders findings made by the Board under Part III of the IR&D Act binding on the Commissioner of Taxation for the purposes of assessing the R&D entity's entitlement to a notional deduction and tax offset under Division 3553.

1.5 The Full Federal Court's Holding and Subsequent Procedural Trajectory
On appeal under section 44 of the Administrative Appeals Tribunal Act 1975 (Cth), the Full Federal Court allowed Moreton Resources' appeal, set aside the Tribunal's decision in [2018] AATA 3378, and remitted the matter to the Tribunal for redetermination in accordance with the law3. Davies, Moshinsky, and Steward JJ held that the Tribunal had misconstrued the statutory gateway in section 355-25(1) by reading in a limitation not found in the legislative text3. At paragraphs [144] to [159], the Full Court set out reasoning that now governs the interpretation of Division 355, which can be distilled into four propositions14. First, the Court held at [148] that the words "experimental activities" in the opening line of section 355-25(1) have very little, if any, work to do beyond reflecting the type of activities described in paragraphs (a) and (b), and at [151] that the Tribunal misconstrued those words by treating them as not covering activities having the purpose of generating new knowledge with respect to the application of an existing technology at a new site; the statutory text is capable of applying, depending on the circumstances, to such activities5. Second, the Court held at [151]–[154] that neither the text of paragraph (b), the exclusions in section 355-25(2), the Explanatory Memorandum, nor the object in section 355-5 supports reading "new knowledge" as excluding knowledge with respect to the application of an existing technology at a new site; paragraph (b) is capable of applying, depending on the circumstances, to such activities, although the Court did not hold that site-specific knowledge will always satisfy paragraph (b)3. Third, although the Court did not expressly rule on the Board's submission that an experiment must be distinguished from merely observing or measuring an unknown quantity by known methods, it stated at [155] (in remarks not dispositive of the appeal) that the Tribunal's view that activities would not be experimental merely because they were a test or trial undertaken for the purpose of discovering something unknown or for testing a principle was "open to doubt", since such activities may, depending on the circumstances, fall within paragraphs (a) and (b) of section 355-25(1)9. Fourth, the Court observed at [133] that, by concluding that the pilot project was not a core R&D activity, the Tribunal had implicitly rejected the taxpayer's alternative submission without determining whether the FY10 registered activities were conducted, whether the FY12–FY14 activities were "directly related" to them, or whether they were undertaken for the "dominant purpose" of supporting them; in obiter remarks at [158]–[159], the Court also noted that the Tribunal appeared to have mischaracterised the pilot project by overlooking the FEED document's stated purpose of demonstrating that the process could be operated in a safe and environmentally responsible manner, that the facility would be the first UCG facility in the world to use a gas turbine to make electricity from syngas, and that the project was conducted under the strict control of the Queensland government to test the environmental impact of the process3. However, the Full Court declined to make the factual determinations under section 355-30 itself, holding at [11] and [160]–[163] that evaluating whether the FY10 activities were core R&D activities, "direct relation", "dominant purpose" (which Moreton accepted it needed to satisfy in addition to section 355-30(1)), and whether the activities were conducted in the registration year would be a factually intensive exercise better undertaken by the Tribunal on remittal10.
Upon remittal, in Moreton Resources Ltd and Industry Innovation and Science Australia [2022] AATA 3804 (decided on 21 September 2022 by Deputy President O'Loughlin), the Tribunal applied the Full Court's statutory construction and ruled largely in favour of the taxpayer6. Deputy President O'Loughlin held that the disputed FY10 registered activity of testing and evaluating gas production and plant performance to ensure environmental standards were met went to the heart of the experimental activities and was not excluded by section 355-25(2)(f), and determined that, with the exception of three activities, the FY12–FY14 activities—including environmental monitoring and rehabilitation, designing and verifying a procedure for rehabilitation of the underground cavity, investigating groundwater movement, ongoing water monitoring, developing processes to decommission the pilot plant, and project management and administration—qualified as eligible "supporting R&D activities" under section 355-30 directly related to the FY10 core R&D activities6.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
While Moreton Resources ultimately prevailed on the question of statutory construction before the Full Federal Court in [2019] FCAFC 120 and on factual remittal in [2022] AATA 3804, the decade-long dispute exposes five profound legal, technical, contractual, and administrative vulnerabilities that routinely trigger regulatory disallowance by IISA/AusIndustry and the Commissioner of Taxation3.
2.1 Mischaracterisation of Post-Incident Remediation and Decommissioning as Stand-Alone "Core R&D Activities"
The primary structural flaw in Moreton Resources' initial FY12–FY14 registrations was its primary contention that post-incident activities—specifically ongoing groundwater monitoring, hydrogeological modelling, cavity rehabilitation design, and pilot plant decommissioning—were themselves stand-alone "core R&D activities" under section 355-25(1)3. For an activity to qualify as a core R&D activity in a given income year, it must independently exhibit a systematic progression of work proceeding from a scientific hypothesis to an experiment, observation, evaluation, and logical conclusion conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge7.
When an experimental pilot plant suffers a catastrophic mechanical failure and is shut down by environmental regulators, the subsequent monitoring of groundwater bores for benzene and toluene and the flushing or rehabilitation of the underground cavity are reactive engineering and environmental management measures3. By registering those FY12–FY14 activities primarily as core R&D activities rather than structuring them from the outset as "supporting R&D activities" under section 355-30 anchored to the FY10 pilot plant core experiment, the taxpayer invited AusIndustry and Deputy President Forgie in the first AAT hearing ([2018] AATA 3378) to scrutinise routine water sampling protocols against the strict experimental gateway of section 355-25(1)(a)3. Although the taxpayer preserved its position via an alternative legal submission linking the FY12–FY14 work to the FY10 core activities, claimants that fail to articulate this core-to-supporting hierarchy in their contemporaneous section 27A registration applications frequently suffer complete disallowance3.
2.2 Triggering the Section 355-25(2)(f) Statutory Compliance Exclusion Without "Dominant Purpose" Segregation
A critical statutory obstacle identified in the litigation was the operation of section 355-25(2)(f) of the ITAA 1997, which expressly excludes from core R&D activities "activities associated with complying with statutory requirements or standards, including ... routine testing and analysis of materials, components, products, processes, soils, atmospheres and other things"3. Following the March 2010 shutdown and the EPO issued by DERM on 17 July 2010, Moreton Resources' groundwater monitoring, cavity rehabilitation, and site remediation during FY12, FY13, and FY14 were carried out under the legal compulsion of its environmental authority (as amended on 7 July 2011 to limit approved activities to decommissioning, rehabilitation, care, and maintenance of the site), the EPO, and Environmental Evaluation Notices issued by the Queensland regulator; the Tribunal's finding that many of these activities were excluded by section 355-25(2)(f) was not challenged before the Full Court3.
As Australian tax jurisprudence confirms, the statutory compliance exclusion in section 355-25(2)(f) is cast in broad terms: it captures all activities associated with compliance and is not restricted to activities conducted for the sole purpose of compliance12. Consequently, once an activity falls within section 355-25(2)(f), it is statutorily barred from being a core R&D activity and can only be rescued as a "supporting R&D activity" if it satisfies the stringent "dominant purpose" test in section 355-30(2)3. Under section 355-30(2), the taxpayer bears the legal burden of proving that the excluded compliance activity was undertaken for the dominant purpose—meaning the ruling, prevailing, or most influential purpose—of supporting the core R&D activities, rather than merely discharging a general commercial or environmental licence obligation3. In Moreton Resources, the taxpayer only overcame this hurdle on remittal in [2022] AATA 3804, where the Tribunal found that its FY12–FY14 activities were directly related to the FY10 core R&D activities (rejecting the regulator's contention that intervening events had changed the nature of the activities); the taxpayer's registrations had described a dedicated pilot plant constructed and used solely for conducting R&D activities, and its environmental authority had from the outset required a shutdown procedure, cavity flushing, removal of residual pollutants, and rehabilitation and monitoring upon cessation of the trial6. Where a taxpayer conducts trials within an active commercial mine or manufacturing plant without physical and documentary segregation, environmental compliance costs will fail the dominant purpose test4.
2.3 Framing Project Objectives Around "Commercial Viability" and "Known Technology"
The dispute before the AAT and the Full Federal Court was heavily precipitated by how the project's overarching objective was described in corporate and regulatory communications. The taxpayer's own documents described the pilot project as testing the viability of using UCG technology at the Kingaroy site, its registrations referred to "integrating known technologies", and the Independent Scientific Panel recorded that the taxpayer had stated it was running not a pilot trial of a new technology but a small-scale facility of well-tested technology; these statements allowed ISA to argue that the project merely tested or observed the results of applying an existing technology at a particular site rather than constituting scientific experimentation3.
In the first AAT decision ([2018] AATA 3378), Deputy President Forgie concluded that the pilot project was "testing the application of existing technology at a particular site and nothing more", while ISA relied on paragraph [2.18] of the Explanatory Memorandum, which states that the knowledge sought must go beyond "merely implementing existing knowledge in a different context or location"3. While the Full Federal Court in [2019] FCAFC 120 overturned that legal error—on the basis of the text, context, and purpose of section 355-25 rather than any finding of its own on the technical facts, while observing in obiter that the Tribunal's characterisation was open to question in light of the FEED document's environmental purpose and the facility's world-first integration of UCG syngas with a gas turbine3—subsequent cases such as GQHC and Commissioner of Taxation [2024] AATA 409 demonstrate the limits of the Moreton Resources principle20. As the Tribunal held in GQHC (and as the ATO emphasised in its Decision Impact Statement), Moreton Resources does not stand for the proposition that applying existing technology to a new environment always generates new knowledge20. If a taxpayer's documentation frames a project around commercial key performance indicators (such as power output, cost per tonne, or yield) rather than formulating explicit scientific hypotheses tying site-specific environmental variables to fundamental physical, chemical, or biological uncertainties, the claim will be disallowed under section 355-25(1)(a) and (b)12.
2.4 Contractual Ambiguity in Licensing Third-Party Proprietary Technology
Moreton Resources obtained a general licence from Canadian firm Ergo Exergy Technologies Inc. to certain of Ergo Exergy's intellectual knowledge regarding the UCG burn process3. In Australian R&D tax audits, the presence of a technology licence agreement or turnkey Engineering, Procurement, and Construction Management (EPCM) contract with an overseas licensor immediately raises two distinct statutory exposures for AusIndustry and the ATO. First, if the licensor warrants the technical performance of the process or provides complete operating parameters, the regulator will contend that the outcome of the process was "known or determined in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information or experience" held by a competent professional (the licensor), violating section 355-25(1)(a)3. Second, if intellectual property or technical know-how generated during site testing reverts exclusively to the foreign licensor or is performed on behalf of another entity, the claimant risks breaching the "conducted for" and intellectual property ownership conditions in section 355-210 of the ITAA 199715.
In Moreton Resources, Ergo Exergy had some expertise with regard to the burn process but no intellectual property in the design, development, and operation of the integrated UCG power generation facility, and the Tribunal accepted that how the UCG process would proceed at any location depended on the particular characteristics of the site and the way the burn process affected it (Golder's pre-ignition report, for example, recorded that the shape of the underground void was largely unknown), although the Tribunal characterised the outcome as one that could be predicted but not known until implementation3. However, where technology licensing agreements are drafted using standard commercial boilerplate—such as clauses stating that the technology is "proven, fully developed, and ready for commercial deployment"—taxpayers create self-inflicted evidentiary wounds that regulators routinely deploy against them in Tribunal proceedings3.
2.5 Cross-Year Registration Disconnects and Post-Litigation Tax Administration Failures
Finally, the Moreton Resources saga highlights acute procedural vulnerabilities across the dual-agency divide between IISA/AusIndustry (administering Part III of the IR&D Act) and the Commissioner of Taxation (administering Division 355 of the ITAA 1997 and the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth) (TAA 1953))3. First, claiming supporting R&D activities in FY12–FY14 based on core R&D activities conducted in FY10 required establishing a direct relationship (and, because the activities fell within a section 355-25(2) exclusion, a dominant purpose of support) spanning the 2010 to 2014 income years pursuant to section 355-30 of the ITAA 1997 and section 27J(1)(c) of the IR&D Act3.
Second, even after achieving a decisive appellate victory in [2019] FCAFC 120 and a favourable AAT finding on remittal in [2022] AATA 3804, the taxpayer suffered a severe procedural setback in late 2023 and 2024 when attempting to secure the actual cash tax offsets from the ATO18. Because the taxpayer's taxation objections under Part IVC of the TAA 1953 had been placed in abeyance pending the resolution of the IR&D Act registration dispute, the taxpayer attempted on 27 December 2023 to reactivate its original objection notice18. However, that attempt was held to be legally invalid because the correspondence failed to strictly comply with the statutory formalities and explicit references required for a notice under section 14ZYA of the TAA 195318. Furthermore, as the Full Federal Court subsequently established in Commissioner of Taxation v Auctus Resources Pty Ltd [2021] FCAFC 39 (and as applied in GQHC [2024] AATA 409), mere registration of activities under section 27A of the IR&D Act does not bind the Commissioner; unless a formal binding Finding is in force under section 355-705, the Commissioner retains full power to independently audit and disallow R&D claims or recover administrative overpayments under section 8AAZN of the TAA 19534.
3. Comparative Summary Table
The following table maps each statutory requirement examined in Moreton Resources Limited v Innovation and Science Australia [2019] FCAFC 120 against the specific legal or evidentiary vulnerability exposed in the dispute and the authoritative standard of proof and statutory construction established by the Full Federal Court3.

Statutory Provision & Legal Requirement
Taxpayer Vulnerability & Regulator / First-Instance AAT Challenge
Full Federal Court Standard of Proof & Authoritative Construction ([2019] FCAFC 120)
Object of Division 355

Section 355-5, ITAA 1997 (Cth)
The first AAT ([2018] AATA 3378) relied on paragraph [1.15] of the Explanatory Memorandum (the taxpayer "needs to do an experiment to discover that knowledge"), and ISA relied on paragraph [2.18] ("merely implementing existing knowledge in a different context or location") and on the object in s 355-5(1), to read down the statutory text and exclude site-specific pilot projects3.
Textual Primacy & Purposive Construction: The statutory text of s 355-25(1) is clear and must be construed in light of the broad object in s 355-5 to encourage industry to conduct scientific, experimental activities that generate new knowledge in a general or applied form3. The Explanatory Memorandum is of limited, if any, assistance and its words cannot be treated as substitutes for the statutory language; to the extent regard may be had to paragraph [2.18], it is not inconsistent with the proposition that, depending on the circumstances, activities generating new knowledge with respect to the application of an existing technology at a new site may fall within the definition9.
Core R&D Activities: Outcome Cannot Be Known in Advance

Section 355-25(1)(a), ITAA 1997 (Cth)
The taxpayer licensed an existing UCG process from Ergo Exergy. ISA argued that because the technology already existed, testing whether it worked at Kingaroy was merely verifying technical/commercial viability rather than resolving an unknown scientific outcome3.
Site-Specific Epistemological Uncertainty: The Court did not separately determine the application of s 355-25(1)(a); it held that the definition is capable of applying, depending on the circumstances, to activities conducted to generate new knowledge with respect to the application of an existing technology at a new site, noting the Tribunal's acceptance that how the UCG process proceeds depends on the particular characteristics of the site, and left the factual application to the Tribunal on remittal3.
Core R&D Activities: Systematic Progression & Scientific Method

Section 355-25(1)(a)(i)–(ii), ITAA 1997 (Cth)
ISA submitted that a legal distinction exists between "conducting an experiment" (testing a hypothesis) and "observing or measuring a phenomenon using established techniques" (e.g., measuring gas composition or groundwater movement)9.
Tribunal's Narrow View Doubted (Obiter): The Court did not expressly rule on the Board's contended distinction, but described as "open to doubt" the Tribunal's view that a test or trial undertaken to discover something unknown or test a principle is not thereby an experimental activity ([155])9. Such activities may, depending on the circumstances, fall within s 355-25(1)(a) and (b), provided the work proceeds systematically from hypothesis to experiment, observation, evaluation, and logical conclusions9.
Core R&D Activities: Purpose of Generating New Knowledge

Section 355-25(1)(b), ITAA 1997 (Cth)
ISA argued that "new knowledge" refers solely to knowledge never previously capable of being known or determined, and the AAT held that the taxpayer was not creating a brand-new product, device, or UCG process3.
No Site-Specific Limitation on "New Knowledge": The text of s 355-25(1)(b) does not impose a limitation excluding knowledge about the application of an existing technology at a new site, and neither the exclusions in s 355-25(2), the Explanatory Memorandum, nor the object in s 355-5 supports such a limitation3. Depending on the circumstances, paragraph (b) is capable of applying to activities conducted to generate new knowledge with respect to the application of an existing technology at a new site; the Court did not, in terms, adopt or reject ISA's "not previously capable of being known or determined" construction3.
Core Exclusions: Complying with Statutory Requirements or Standards

Section 355-25(2)(f), ITAA 1997 (Cth)
In FY12–FY14, the taxpayer registered post-shutdown groundwater monitoring and cavity rehabilitation as core R&D activities while operating under its Queensland environmental authority, the EPO, and Environmental Evaluation Notices3. The AAT held these were excluded under s 355-25(2)(f)3.
Unchallenged Tribunal Finding on Core Exclusion: Moreton did not challenge the Tribunal's conclusion that its registered FY12–FY14 core R&D activities were excluded as activities associated with complying with statutory requirements or standards under s 355-25(2)(f), and the Full Court therefore did not consider that exclusion ([8], [123])3. They can only be claimed if they qualify as supporting R&D activities under s 355-303.
Supporting R&D Activities Across Income Years

Section 355-30(1), ITAA 1997 (Cth) & Section 27J(1)(c), IR&D Act 1986 (Cth)
Because the first AAT concluded that the FY10 pilot project was not a core R&D activity, it dismissed the taxpayer's alternative claim that the FY12–FY14 remediation activities were supporting R&D activities3.
Cross-Year Temporal Nexus Permitted: The Court noted that s 27J(1)(c)(ii) of the IR&D Act allows the Board to find that an activity registered in a later income year (FY12–FY14) was a supporting R&D activity in relation to core R&D activities registered in an earlier income year (FY10), but declined to determine whether Moreton's activities met s 355-30, remitting that factually intensive question to the Tribunal ([23], [163])3. On remittal ([2022] AATA 3804), remediating the failed experimental pilot plant was held to be directly related to the FY10 core experiment6.
Supporting R&D Activities: The "Dominant Purpose" Test

Section 355-30(2), ITAA 1997 (Cth)
Where a supporting activity falls within a s 355-25(2) exclusion (such as s 355-25(2)(f) environmental compliance) or produces goods/services, a simple "direct relation" is insufficient3.
Fact-Intensive Dominant Purpose Threshold: The Court noted that Moreton accepted it needed to satisfy s 355-30(2) in addition to s 355-30(1), and held that determining whether the activities were undertaken for the dominant purpose of supporting the core R&D activities was a factually intensive exercise for the Tribunal ([163])3. On remittal, the Tribunal found that, except for three activities, the FY12–FY14 activities were supporting R&D activities in relation to the FY10 core R&D activities6.

4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies
To translate the appellate principles of Moreton Resources Limited v Innovation and Science Australia [2019] FCAFC 120—together with the subsequent administrative lessons from Moreton Resources [2022] AATA 3804, Commissioner of Taxation v Auctus Resources Pty Ltd [2021] FCAFC 39, and GQHC and Commissioner of Taxation [2024] AATA 409—into actionable legal and technical practice, this section presents two comprehensive Australian industry case studies3. Each case study models a corporate taxpayer confronting the exact statutory pitfalls exposed in the ruling and sets out a four-step remedial blueprint covering project governance, technical documentation, contractual structuring, and experimentation and expenditure tracking.
4.1 Case Study 1: Subsurface In-Situ Copper Recovery (ISCR) & Hydrogeological Containment Pilot in the Australian Resources Sector
Pilbara Leach Dynamics Pty Ltd ("Pilbara Leach"), an Australian corporate taxpayer headquartered in Perth, holds a mineral tenement in the Paterson Province of Western Australia containing a deep, low-grade, fractured-rock copper-gold porphyry deposit situated beneath a hypersaline artesian aquifer. Conventional open-pit or block-cave mining is economically unviable. In the 2025 income year (FY25), Pilbara Leach enters into a technology licence and engineering services agreement with a Chilean metallurgical firm ("AndesTech") to license an established glycinate-lixiviant In-Situ Copper Recovery (ISCR) process that AndesTech has successfully operated in shallow oxide deposits in South America.
Pilbara Leach constructs a five-spot injection-and-recovery borehole array and surface pilot plant in FY25 to test whether the glycinate lixiviant can leach copper in situ from the deep fractured bedrock. Three weeks after injection commences in late FY25, unexpected tectonic fault-valve behaviour causes lixiviant excursion into the upper hypersaline aquifer, triggering precipitation of copper-glycinate complexes that clog the recovery well screens. The Western Australian Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER) issues a statutory Environmental Protection Notice halting injection and requiring Pilbara Leach across FY26 and FY27 to conduct intensive hydrogeological plume modelling, pump-and-treat aquifer flushing, borehole pressure testing, and pilot wellfield decommissioning. Pilbara Leach's internal accounting team proposes to register the entire FY25, FY26, and FY27 expenditure as "core R&D activities" under section 355-25(1), describing the project in its draft AusIndustry application as "Trialing AndesTech's proven ISCR technology to confirm the commercial and technical viability of leaching copper at the Paterson site and complying with DWER aquifer remediation directives."
If lodged in this form, Pilbara Leach's claim faces almost certain disallowance by IISA/AusIndustry and the ATO due to four acute Moreton Resources pitfalls. First, framing the FY25 pilot around "confirming commercial and technical viability" of "proven ISCR technology" invites disallowance under section 355-25(1)(a) and (b) as routine site adaptation of existing knowledge3. Second, including preliminary resource definition drilling risks contamination by the mineral exploration and drilling exclusion in section 355-25(2)(b)3. Third, registering the FY26–FY27 DWER-mandated aquifer flushing and monitoring as core R&D activities triggers immediate disqualification under the statutory compliance exclusion in section 355-25(2)(f)3. Fourth, failing to structure the FY26–FY27 remediation as supporting R&D activities under section 355-30(1) and (2) anchored to the FY25 core experiment leaves the taxpayer without contemporaneous evidence of "dominant purpose"3.
4.2 Remedial Restructuring Blueprint for Case Study 1
To overcome these statutory barriers and satisfy Division 355, Pilbara Leach must execute a four-stage restructuring programme across project governance, technical documentation, contractual architecture, and accounting substantiation.
In Step 1 (Project Governance and Dual-Agency Regulatory Strategy), prior to lodging its section 27A registration for FY25 and prior to executing the FY26–FY27 remediation workstreams, Pilbara Leach must constitute an internal R&D Tax Governance Committee comprising the Principal Hydrogeologist, Chief Metallurgist, Chief Financial Officer, and external Australian R&D tax counsel4. The Committee must enact a binding R&D Charter mandating that no expenditure be coded to Division 355 general ledger accounts without a signed Core & Supporting Activity Scoping Protocol4. Acting under this charter, the Committee must ruthlessly excise all preliminary geological resource definition drilling and JORC-compliance core logging from the Division 355 registration, treating those costs under standard income tax provisions (Subdivision 40-H exploration expenditure deductions) so that the section 355-25(2)(b) exploration exclusion does not taint the pilot wellfield claim3. Furthermore, to neutralise the dual-agency audit risk identified in Auctus Resources [2021] FCAFC 39 and GQHC [2024] AATA 409—whereby the ATO can unilaterally disallow registered activities in the absence of a binding Board finding—Pilbara Leach should apply to IISA under section 28A of the IR&D Act for an Advance Finding confirming that the FY25 pilot wellfield trial is an eligible core R&D activity and that the lifecycle aquifer containment and decommissioning obligations are eligible supporting R&D activities4. Once issued, a positive Advance Finding binds the Commissioner of Taxation under section 355-705 of the ITAA 1997 for up to three income years3. Additionally, should any assessment dispute arise, external tax counsel must maintain a calendarised Part IVC litigation register to ensure that any taxation objections and section 14ZYA notices under the TAA 1953 are validly drafted and cross-referenced, avoiding the procedural invalidation suffered by Moreton Resources in December 202318.
In Step 2 (Technical Documentation and Hypothesis Formulation), to bring the project squarely within paragraphs [148]–[151] of Moreton Resources [2019] FCAFC 120, Pilbara Leach must purge all references to "confirming commercial viability" from its technical scoping documents and AusIndustry registration3. Instead, the Principal Hydrogeologist must author a comprehensive Baseline Literature Review & Gap Analysis prior to pilot ignition demonstrating why a competent professional cannot determine the outcome of applying AndesTech's glycinate ISCR process to the Paterson deposit in advance on the basis of current global knowledge, information, or experience under section 355-25(1)(a)3. Specifically, the technical dossier must contrast AndesTech's historical deployment (shallow, low-salinity, oxidised porphyry zones at less than 150 metres depth) with the Paterson site's unique physical parameters (deep primary chalcopyrite-bornite mineralisation at 650 metres depth, high confining lithostatic stress of , and interaction with a hypersaline magnesium-chloride briny aquifer exceeding  TDS)5. The documentation must formulate explicit, testable scientific hypotheses under section 355-25(1)(a)(ii) and define the precise applied "new knowledge" sought under section 355-25(1)(b)3. For the FY25 Core R&D Activity, the formal hypothesis must state that injecting an alkaline copper-glycinate lixiviant (, dissolved oxygen ) into fractured primary chalcopyrite-bornite bedrock under  hydrostatic head and  TDS brine interface can achieve selective copper dissolution ( extraction kinetics) without inducing divalent cation () gypsum or carbonate scaling or fault-induced hydraulic short-circuiting across the confining aquitard. Where the unexpected fault-valve failure in FY25 prompts genuinely novel experimental investigations in FY26 to develop a new synthetic polymer-silicate grouting formulation to seal hypersaline fractured rock under high pressure, that specific experimental development must be documented as a separate FY26 Core R&D Activity with its own hypothesis, experimental test matrix, observation logs, and evaluation report3. Conversely, all routine bore water sampling, pump-and-treat flushing, and wellfield decommissioning required under the DWER Environmental Protection Notice must be strictly classified in the technical dossier as Supporting R&D Activities under section 355-30(1) and (2) supporting the FY25 Core R&D Activity3.
In Step 3 (Contract Terms and IP / Licensing Structuring), to prevent AusIndustry from using the AndesTech licence agreement as evidence that the technology's outcome was known in advance, Pilbara Leach's legal counsel must restructure the Technology Licence and Engineering Services Agreement prior to execution3. First, the contract must incorporate an explicit disclaimer of site-specific performance warranties in its Preamble and Technical Schedule, reciting that AndesTech's proprietary baseline intellectual property has never been validated in deep, high-stress, hypersaline primary sulphide formations, and that AndesTech provides no warranty or performance guarantee regarding leaching kinetics, lixiviant stability, or hydraulic containment at the Paterson site3. Second, the intellectual property clauses must clearly delineate baseline IP from foreground applied knowledge, vesting beneficial ownership of all site-specific experimental data, hydrogeological models, modified lixiviant formulations, and high-pressure grouting protocols generated during the Australian trials in Pilbara Leach, thereby satisfying the "conducted for" and ownership requirements of section 355-210 of the ITAA 199715. Third, the pilot plant construction contract and state tenement approval deeds must include an environmental lifecycle obligation clause explicitly recording that the five-spot pilot wellfield is a temporary, non-commercial experimental facility that is legally barred from producing commercial copper cathode and must be fully rehabilitated and decommissioned upon conclusion of the experimental test programme6.
In Step 4 (Experimentation Tracking, Cost Apportionment, and Multi-Year Supporting Substantiation), during project execution across FY25, FY26, and FY27, Pilbara Leach must implement rigorous contemporaneous record-keeping to satisfy the evidentiary standards applied on remittal in Moreton Resources [2022] AATA 3804, as detailed in the structured compliance matrix below5.

4.3 Case Study 2: Industrial Bioprocessing & PFAS Thermal-Catalytic Destruction Pilot Plant in the Australian Manufacturing & Environmental Engineering Sector
EnviroSynth Manufacturing Ltd ("EnviroSynth"), an Australian chemical engineering and waste-valorisation company operating in Victoria, processes organic industrial biosolids into commercial soil-conditioning pellets at its Dandenong facility. In the 2025 income year (FY25), EnviroSynth seeks to address per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination in incoming municipal biosolids while simultaneously producing marketable biochar. EnviroSynth acquires a commercial off-the-shelf rotary pyrolysis kiln from a German manufacturer and retrofits it with an experimental, proprietary bimetallic steam-reforming catalyst bed designed to cleave carbon-fluorine () bonds in short-chain perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) at reduced temperatures ( instead of ).
During FY25, EnviroSynth processes 12,000 tonnes of biosolids through the modified pyrolysis kiln, selling the resulting uncontaminated biochar output to agricultural wholesalers for A$1.8 million. Late in FY25, aggressive hydrogen fluoride () off-gas corrosion causes a refractory lining collapse inside the catalytic chamber, releasing trace fluorinated dioxins into the plant's wet-scrubber effluent tank. Environment Protection Authority (EPA) Victoria issues a statutory Clean-Up Notice requiring EnviroSynth throughout FY26 to conduct continuous stack-gas and scrubber-water fluorochemical assays, replace the corroded scrubber vessels, and chemically neutralise and dispose of 4,000 kilolitres of contaminated scrubber sludge. EnviroSynth's external accountant registers the entire FY25 plant operating costs (including all 12,000 tonnes of biosolid processing) and all FY26 EPA clean-up and vessel replacement costs as "core R&D activities", without calculating any feedstock adjustment and without segregating routine commercial production or EPA statutory compliance.
This claim is acutely vulnerable to disallowance and tax penalties across four fronts identified in Moreton Resources [2019] FCAFC 120, Auctus Resources [2021] FCAFC 39, and GQHC [2024] AATA 409. First, processing 12,000 tonnes of commercial biosolids in a German rotary kiln blurs the boundary between testing an existing pyrolysis technology and conducting specific experimental trials on the bimetallic catalyst bed, risking total disallowance under GQHC [2024] AATA 4094. Second, claiming the processing of commercial outputs without proving a "dominant purpose" under section 355-30(2) for non-experimental runs and failing to calculate a mandatory feedstock adjustment under section 355-445 (former section 355-465) on the A$1.8 million of marketable biochar exposes the company to full tax shortfall clawbacks4. Third, registering the FY26 EPA-mandated effluent assays and sludge disposal as core R&D activities directly contravenes the statutory compliance exclusion in section 355-25(2)(f)3. Fourth, because EnviroSynth operates a commercial facility at Dandenong, replacing corroded wet-scrubber vessels used for ongoing commercial production in FY26 will fail the "dominant purpose" test in section 355-30(2) unless the experimental pilot line is physically and operationally segregated from commercial production3.
4.4 Remedial Restructuring Blueprint for Case Study 2
To achieve full compliance with Division 355 and insulate the claim from audit disallowance, EnviroSynth must implement a four-step restructuring methodology across its operational governance, scientific documentation, vendor contracting, and tax accounting.
In Step 1 (Physical and Operational Segregation via Project Governance), to insulate its R&D claim from commercial production and compliance exclusions, EnviroSynth's Board of Directors must establish a formal R&D Governance & Trial Segregation Protocol prior to commencing FY25 testing4. Rather than running continuous commercial biosolid batches through the modified kiln and claiming the entire 12,000-tonne campaign as core R&D, the Governance Committee must mandate strict batch and campaign segregation4. Specifically, EnviroSynth must designate 15 discrete, instrumented 48-hour test runs (totalling 600 tonnes of spiked biosolid feedstock) conducted under varying temperature ( to ), residence time, and catalyst-to-steam ratios as the dedicated Core R&D Activity under section 355-25(1)4. The remaining 11,400 tonnes of standard biosolid processing conducted using fixed operating parameters must be classified as ordinary commercial production, coded to standard cost-of-goods-sold (COGS) accounts, and excluded entirely from the Division 355 claim4. Furthermore, following the refractory lining failure in the experimental catalytic chamber, EnviroSynth must physically isolate the experimental catalytic skid and its dedicated holding tank from the main commercial plant scrubber line so that the FY26 decontamination and decommissioning of the experimental catalytic reactor can satisfy the "dominant purpose" test in section 355-30(2) in accordance with Moreton Resources [2022] AATA 38044.
In Step 2 (Technical Documentation Distinguishing Moreton Resources from GQHC), to overcome the ATO's post-GQHC scrutiny of "existing technology in a new environment"20, EnviroSynth's Chief Chemical Engineer must author a rigorous Scientific Protocol & Hypothesis Dossier prior to the 15 experimental runs. The dossier must acknowledge that rotary kiln pyrolysis of biosolids is an established technology, thereby focusing the section 355-25(1) core activity boundary strictly on the scientifically unknown reaction kinetics of the retrofitted bimetallic steam-reforming catalyst bed when exposed to complex, heterogeneous Australian municipal biosolid matrices containing competing sulphur and chloride poisons9. The dossier must state an explicit, falsifiable scientific hypothesis under section 355-25(1)(a)(ii): namely, that introducing superheated steam () across a nickel-cerium-zirconia bimetallic catalyst bed within the secondary pyrolysis gas zone at  will promote hydrodefluorination of vaporised short-chain PFBA () to achieve  mineralisation into inorganic fluoride ions () without rapid catalyst deactivation via hydrogen sulphide () poisoning from biosolid proteins. Moreover, drawing on the Full Federal Court's observation in Moreton Resources [2019] FCAFC 120 (at [155]) that a test or trial undertaken for the purpose of discovering something unknown or testing a principle may, depending on the circumstances, satisfy section 355-25(1)(a) and (b), including where established analytical techniques (such as High-Performance Liquid Chromatography–Tandem Mass Spectrometry, HPLC-MS/MS, and Ion Chromatography) are used to observe and measure an unknown experimental outcome9, EnviroSynth must document how each HPLC-MS/MS fluorochemical assay during the 15 experimental runs directly tests and evaluates the hydrodefluorination hypothesis.
In Step 3 (Contractual Restructuring with Equipment Vendors and Environmental Contractors), EnviroSynth must restructure its procurement and environmental remediation contracts to align with the statutory requirements of Division 355. First, under the German rotary kiln procurement and modification contracts, the purchase agreement for the base rotary kiln must separate the capital cost of the standard kiln (claimed only via tax depreciation decline in value under section 355-305 for the exact time-apportioned hours used in the 15 experimental runs) from the custom engineering fabrication contract for the experimental bimetallic catalytic reactor chamber12. The fabrication contract must specify that EnviroSynth retains sole intellectual property ownership and bears all technical and financial risk for the catalytic chamber design15. Second, when engaging specialist environmental contractors in FY26 to neutralise the fluorinated scrubber sludge and decommission the failed catalytic chamber under the EPA Clean-Up Notice, the contractual Scope of Work must bifurcate invoices into two separate schedules: Schedule A covering the isolated experimental catalytic reactor and its dedicated 400-kilolitre experimental effluent tank (linked exclusively to the FY25 core experiment), and Schedule B covering general plant-wide EPA compliance monitoring and scrubber replacement for the commercial Dandenong facility4.
In Step 4 (Experimentation Tracking, Feedstock Adjustment Calculation, and Multi-Year Supporting Substantiation), to ensure full audit defensibility before both IISA/AusIndustry and the ATO, EnviroSynth must execute a precise accounting and substantiation protocol across FY25 and FY26. During the 15 core experimental runs in FY25 (600 tonnes out of 12,000 tonnes total annual throughput, representing exactly 5.0 per cent of operating hours), operator wages, laboratory HPLC-MS/MS testing fees, bimetallic catalyst consumables, and 5.0 per cent of kiln energy and Division 40 decline-in-value depreciation are coded to GL-355-Core-FY254. Because the 600 tonnes of biosolids processed during those 15 core experimental runs are transformed into marketable biochar sold to agricultural wholesalers for A1.8 million total biochar revenue), EnviroSynth must calculate and include a mandatory feedstock adjustment in its FY25 company tax return under section 355-445 (former section 355-465), bringing into assessable income (or reducing the notional deduction by) the lesser of the feedstock output revenue (A$90,000) and the eligible feedstock input expenditure incurred during those 15 experimental runs4. Finally, in its FY26 AusIndustry registration, EnviroSynth registers the decontamination, refractory failure forensic analysis, and neutralisation of the isolated 400-kilolitre experimental tank (Schedule A) as a Supporting R&D Activity under section 355-30, explicitly cross-referenced to the FY25 Core R&D Activity pursuant to section 27J(1)(c) of the IR&D Act3. Because those activities are associated with complying with the EPA Clean-Up Notice (an exclusion under section 355-25(2)(f)), EnviroSynth prepares a contemporaneous Section 355-30(2) Dominant Purpose Substantiation File containing engineering P&ID schematics proving that the experimental catalytic reactor and its 400-kilolitre tank were physically isolated from commercial production and that their decontamination was caused solely by the unexpected  refractory collapse during the FY25 core experiment3. Conversely, all Schedule B plant-wide commercial EPA monitoring costs are excluded from the R&D claim and deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 8-1 of the ITAA 19974.

5. Synthesis of Legal Principles and Strategic Conclusions
The Full Federal Court's ruling in Moreton Resources Limited v Innovation and Science Australia [2019] FCAFC 120 remains the cornerstone of taxpayer protection against overly narrow administrative interpretations of Division 355 of the ITAA 19973. By confirming that the statutory definition of "core R&D activities" in section 355-25(1) is capable, depending on the circumstances, of encompassing activities conducted to generate new knowledge with respect to the application of an existing technology at a new site—and by casting doubt on the Tribunal's view that a test or trial undertaken to discover something unknown or test a principle is not thereby an experimental activity—the Full Court realigned the administration of the R&D Tax Incentive with its statutory object in section 355-53. Equally important, the Court's remittal of the cross-year "supporting R&D activities" question under section 355-30, culminating in the taxpayer's largely successful outcome on remittal in [2022] AATA 3804, established that mandatory environmental remediation and decommissioning of a failed experimental pilot plant are legitimate supporting costs of industrial innovation3.
Nevertheless, as subsequent jurisprudence in Commissioner of Taxation v Auctus Resources Pty Ltd [2021] FCAFC 39 and GQHC and Commissioner of Taxation [2024] AATA 409—alongside Moreton Resources' own post-remittal Part IVC procedural difficulties—makes clear, appellate precedent cannot rescue a claim that lacks rigorous contemporaneous substantiation or procedural discipline4. Corporate claimants and their tax advisors in Australia must ensure that site-specific uncertainties are framed around falsifiable scientific hypotheses rather than commercial viability, that technology licensing contracts explicitly disclaim site-specific performance guarantees, that statutory compliance and remediation activities are properly classified under section 355-30(2) with ring-fenced evidence of "dominant purpose", and that dual-agency administrative procedures under the IR&D Act and the TAA 1953 are executed with strict statutory precision3.
